title: College Sport as Two Sentences
bigQuestion: Is a college athlete a student who plays, a worker who studies, or something the law has not yet named?

story.title: Two Papers in One Locker
story.kicker: One sheet lists a player's classes; the other sells the same player to the public.
paragraphs: A sophomore opens a locker in a college football building. Taped inside the door is a class schedule: biology at 8 a.m., writing at 10, statistics after lunch. Next to it sits the team's media guide. The guide lists the same young woman or man by height, hometown, jersey number and high school honors.

The two papers describe one person in two ways. The schedule treats her as a student who must pass enough classes to stay eligible. The media guide treats her as part of a product that the school sells to fans, sponsors and television networks. Both papers carry the university's name and seal.

Since 1991, NCAA rules have capped required practice and team activity in season at 20 hours a week. Travel, treatment for injuries and film study on a player's own time are often not counted. Students and coaches have argued for decades about what that cap means in a real week.

Down the hall, a staff member checks the eligibility list. It tracks grades, credit hours and progress toward a degree. A player who falls behind in class can be benched without ever missing a practice. The list is a school record and a team record at the same time.

The sophomore closes the locker. The schedule says she is here to learn. The media guide says she is here to play. American courts, the NCAA and state lawmakers have spent more than a century deciding which paper tells the truth.
story.think: If one person is described by both papers, which one should decide the rules about pay, injury and school?

lessons.title: A Race Paid For by a Railroad
lessons.mainIdea: The first college contests in the United States, a Harvard–Yale rowing race in 1852 and a Rutgers–Princeton football game in 1869, were run by students, and one was sponsored by a business.
reading: The first *intercollegiate* contest in the United States was a rowing race. In August 1852, crews from Harvard and Yale raced on Lake Winnipesaukee in New Hampshire. Intercollegiate means between two or more colleges. Harvard won. The race was not organized by professors or deans.

A railroad company, the Boston, Concord and Montreal Railroad, paid the crews' travel and lodging. The railroad hoped the race would draw tourists to the lake and fill its trains. So the very first college contest in the country was also a piece of *commercial* advertising. Commercial means done to make money.

On November 6, 1869, Rutgers and Princeton played the first intercollegiate football game in New Brunswick, New Jersey. Rutgers won, 6 goals to 4. The rules looked more like soccer than modern football. Each side had 25 players, and the students agreed on the rules among themselves before the game.

For the rest of the 1800s, students ran most college sport through their own clubs and associations. They booked games, raised money and hired trainers. Faculty and college presidents began to step in only when games grew large, costly and sometimes violent.

words.d: between two or more colleges, such as a game between two schools' teams
done to make money, such as advertising or selling tickets
organized and paid for by students rather than by the college

look.title: Who Paid for the First Race?
look.text: Summer, 1852. Two college boat crews arrive at a New Hampshire lake. They did not buy their own train tickets or hotel rooms. A railroad company paid. The company expected crowds of visitors who would ride its trains to watch.
look.prompt: What did the railroad want from the race, and what did the students get? Name one way this looks like college sport today.

check.q: What was the first intercollegiate contest in the United States?
check.why: Harvard and Yale crews raced on Lake Winnipesaukee in August 1852.

check.q: Why did a railroad pay for the 1852 race?
choices: A law required it to support colleges.
It hoped the race would bring riders to its trains.
The college presidents asked for a donation.
check.why: The Boston, Concord and Montreal Railroad hoped to sell trips to the lake.

check.q: Who set the rules for the 1869 Rutgers–Princeton game?
choices: the students of the two schools
check.why: Students agreed on rules among themselves; the NCAA did not exist until 1906.

lessons.title: Professors Take Charge in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895, university leaders met in Chicago to put faculty in control of college athletics, forming the conference later called the Big Ten.
reading: By the 1890s, college football drew big crowds and big money. Some teams used players who were not real students. Some paid players in secret. Purdue president James H. Smart invited leaders from several Midwestern universities to meet in Chicago in January 1895 to write common rules.

Seven schools joined the new group: Chicago, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, Northwestern, Purdue and Wisconsin. Its formal name was the Intercollegiate Conference of Faculty Representatives. People called it the Western Conference. A *conference* is a group of schools that agree to play each other under shared rules. It is known today as the Big Ten.

The key idea was *faculty control*. Each school sent a professor, not a coach or a student, to the conference. The early rules said a player had to be a real student in good standing. They also limited how long someone could keep playing for a college team.

The University of Chicago was a founding power in the conference. Its president, William Rainey Harper, hired Amos Alonzo Stagg in 1892 and gave him a place on the faculty, which was unusual for a coach. Chicago later stepped back. It dropped football after the 1939 season and left the conference in 1946.

words.d: a group of schools that agree to play each other under shared rules
the idea that professors, not coaches or students, should make the rules for college sport
being enrolled and keeping up with the school's academic rules

look.title: Founding Schools and Their Home States

look.prompt: Which state had the most founding schools, and why might a meeting in Chicago make sense for this group?

check.q: What was the main idea behind the 1895 Chicago meeting?
choices: putting professors in control of college sport
check.why: The conference was built on faculty control: each school sent a professor.

check.q: Which of these was a founding school of the Western Conference?
check.why: Northwestern was one of the seven founders in 1895, along with Chicago and Illinois.

check.q: What happened to the University of Chicago's place in the conference?
choices: It founded a rival league in 1920.
It dropped football after 1939 and left the conference in 1946.
check.why: Chicago ended football after the 1939 season and withdrew in 1946.

lessons.title: A Crisis and a New Body
lessons.mainIdea: Deaths and injuries in football in 1905 led to a White House meeting and to a new national body in 1906, renamed the NCAA in 1910.
reading: College football in the early 1900s was rough. Players wore little padding, and mass plays piled bodies on top of each other. Newspapers kept counts of players killed in college and school games. In 1905, published counts listed about 18 deaths. Some colleges, including Columbia, dropped the sport.

On October 9, 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt invited coaches and advisers from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House. He urged them to clean up the game. Roosevelt liked football and did not want it banned. The meeting brought publicity but no new rules.

In November 1905, a Union College player, Harold Moore, died after an injury in a game against New York University. NYU chancellor Henry MacCracken then called college leaders to meet in New York in December. Dozens of colleges took part. On March 31, 1906, they formed the Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States, or *IAAUS*.

The IAAUS rules committee changed football in 1906. It legalized the forward pass and set a longer distance for a first down. In 1910 the IAAUS took a new name, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or *NCAA*. It started as a rule-making body. Over time it also became a governing body that runs championships and decides who is *eligible* to play.

words.d: the Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States, founded in 1906
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, the IAAUS's name since 1910
allowed under the rules to play or compete
an organization that writes and enforces the rules for a sport or group

look.title: Three Ways to Answer a Crisis
look.text: Fall 1905. One college drops football entirely. The President of the United States asks three schools to clean it up by themselves. A university chancellor calls every college he can reach to a meeting and proposes one shared set of rules and one national body.
look.prompt: Which of the three answers created a lasting institution? Why might the other two have been less likely to last?

check.q: What did President Roosevelt do in October 1905?
choices: He invited leaders from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House.
He signed a law limiting football deaths.
check.why: Roosevelt met with Harvard, Yale and Princeton leaders on October 9, 1905, but did not ban the game.

check.q: What was the NCAA called when it was founded in 1906?
check.why: It was the Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States until 1910.

check.q: Which rule change came in 1906?
choices: Freshmen were barred from all sports.
check.why: The 1906 rules committee legalized the forward pass.

lessons.title: The Amateur Promise
lessons.mainIdea: College sport was built on the idea that players are amateurs, but critics from the 1890s on, a 1929 report and later NCAA rules showed how hard that promise was to keep.
reading: An *amateur* is someone who plays without being paid. In the late 1800s, the amateur ideal came to American colleges from English schools and clubs. Many of those clubs had also used amateur rules to keep working-class athletes out. The ideal said sport should build character, not income.

American colleges struggled to live up to the ideal. In the 1890s, critics complained about *tramp athletes*. These were players who moved from college to college to play for whoever offered the most, sometimes without attending classes. Conference rules on residence and good standing were written partly to stop them. In 1905, journalist Henry Beach Needham described hidden recruiting and payments in a series called The College Athlete in McClure's Magazine.

In October 1929, the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching published a report called American College Athletics. Its team, led by Howard J. Savage, visited more than 100 colleges. It found widespread *recruiting* and secret payments to athletes. It blamed college leaders for allowing sport to become a business.

The NCAA tried to write the ideal into rules. In 1948 it adopted the Sanity Code, which limited aid to athletes to tuition and fees and tied it to need. In 1950, an attempt to expel seven schools that admitted breaking the code failed to get enough votes. The NCAA dropped the code in 1951.

words.d: a player who takes part without receiving pay
a college player of the late 1800s who moved from school to school to play, sometimes without taking classes
persuading an athlete to come to a school to play for its team
the NCAA's 1948 rules limiting aid to athletes, dropped in 1951

look.title: What the Carnegie Report Found
look.text: The report found that many colleges recruited athletes and paid them in hidden ways, such as jobs that required little work. It said college presidents and trustees shared the blame, because they let athletics grow into a commercial enterprise.
look.cite: Howard J. Savage and others, American College Athletics, Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, Bulletin No. 23, 1929
look.prompt: Whom did the report hold responsible? Why does that matter for who should fix the problem?

check.q: What is an amateur athlete?
choices: an athlete who plays without being paid
an athlete who plays only one sport
an athlete who has not yet won a game
check.why: Amateur means competing without pay.

check.q: What was a tramp athlete in the 1890s?
choices: a coach who worked for several colleges
a player who moved from college to college to play, sometimes without taking classes
a runner who competed only on roads
a student manager who carried equipment
check.why: Critics used the term for players who drifted between colleges to play, which conference rules tried to stop.

check.q: What happened to the NCAA's Sanity Code?
choices: It is still in force today.
It was written by the Carnegie Foundation.
It was dropped in 1951 after a vote to expel seven schools failed.
check.why: The 1948 code could not be enforced and was dropped in 1951.

lessons.title: Scholarships, Grades and Freshmen
lessons.mainIdea: From 1956 onward the NCAA allowed athletic scholarships, then kept changing rules on how long they last and what grades a player needs.
reading: In 1956 the NCAA allowed full *athletic scholarships* for the first time. A school could now pay tuition, fees, room, board and books for a student because of athletic skill. The rule also allowed a small allowance, often remembered as 15 dollars a month for laundry. Before this, open athletic aid had been against NCAA rules.

In 1973 the NCAA ruled that athletic scholarships would last one year and be renewed each year. A coach could decline to renew a player's aid. In 2012 the NCAA again allowed schools to offer multi-year scholarships. In 2015 the largest conferences agreed to cover the full *cost of attendance*, including living costs.

Freshmen were long barred from varsity teams so they could settle into college. The NCAA let freshmen play most varsity sports in 1968. It extended that to football and basketball in 1972. In 1973 the NCAA also split its members into Division I, Division II and Division III.

Grades became a gate too. Proposition 48, adopted in 1983 and in force in 1986, set *initial eligibility* rules. A freshman needed a 2.0 grade point average in 11 core high school courses and a minimum SAT or ACT score. Critics said test cutoffs hurt Black students most. In 1989 Georgetown coach John Thompson walked off the court before a game to protest a stricter follow-up rule, Proposition 42.

words.d: money a college gives a student to pay for school because of athletic skill
the full price of attending college, including tuition, housing, food and living costs
the rules a new college athlete must meet to play in the first year
the NCAA rule, adopted in 1983, that set minimum grades and test scores for freshman athletes

look.title: When Scholarship and Freshman Rules Changed
rows: Freshmen allowed in most varsity sports
Freshmen allowed in football and basketball
Scholarships limited to one year at a time
look.cite: NCAA convention records and legislative history
look.prompt: How many years passed between one-year scholarships and the return of multi-year scholarships? What might that mean for a player's security?

check.q: In what year did the NCAA first allow full athletic scholarships?
check.why: The NCAA approved full athletic grants-in-aid in 1956.

check.q: What did the 1973 scholarship rule change?
choices: Scholarships became one-year awards renewed each year.
Scholarships were paid by the federal government.
check.why: From 1973, athletic aid lasted one year, and a coach could decline to renew it.

check.q: What did Proposition 48 set?
choices: minimum grades and test scores for freshman athletes
the size of the basketball tournament
check.why: Proposition 48 set a 2.0 average in 11 core courses and a minimum test score.

lessons.title: Doors Shut and Doors Opened
lessons.mainIdea: Black athletes and women were long kept out of college sport or given separate places, and those doors opened unevenly through the 1900s.
reading: A few Black athletes played for Northern colleges early on. Fritz Pollard of Brown University played in the Rose Bowl on January 1, 1916. Paul Robeson was named an All-American at Rutgers in 1917 and 1918. They faced taunts and violence on the field. Most Southern colleges kept their teams all white by rule and by custom.

*Segregation* reached Northern teams too. Some Northern schools benched their Black players when a Southern team refused to play against them. In October 1934, Michigan kept Willis Ward out of a game against Georgia Tech for that reason. Black colleges built their own conferences. The Colored Intercollegiate Athletic Association, now the CIAA, was founded in 1912.

On March 19, 1966, Texas Western College started five Black players in the NCAA men's basketball final. It beat an all-white University of Kentucky team coached by Adolph Rupp. The game was a turning point. Southern conferences that had not yet done so added Black athletes over the following years.

Women's college sport grew under a separate body. The Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women, or *AIAW*, was founded in 1971 and ran national championships. *Title IX* of the Education Amendments of 1972 barred sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money. The NCAA began women's championships in 1981–82, and the AIAW closed in 1982.

words.d: keeping people apart by race, by law or by custom
the women's college sports body that held national championships from 1971 to 1982
the 1972 federal law that bars sex discrimination in education programs that get federal money

look.title: A Benched Player in 1934
look.text: Michigan, October 1934. Willis Ward is one of the team's best players. Georgia Tech says it will not play if a Black player takes the field. Michigan agrees to keep Ward out. Some Michigan students and teammates protest. The game goes on without him.
look.prompt: Which school made the decision to bench Ward? What does this show about how segregation reached places that had no segregation law?

check.q: What happened in the 1966 NCAA men's basketball final?
choices: The AIAW held its first championship.
Brown played in the Rose Bowl.
Texas Western started five Black players and beat all-white Kentucky.
check.why: Texas Western's win on March 19, 1966, was a turning point in integrating college sport.

check.q: What was the AIAW?
choices: a Black college conference founded in 1912
a body that ran women's college championships from 1971 to 1982
check.why: The AIAW governed women's college sport until the NCAA took over women's championships.

check.q: Why did Michigan keep Willis Ward out of a 1934 game?
choices: Georgia Tech refused to play against a Black player.
Ward had been paid to play.
A Michigan state law required it.
check.why: Michigan gave in to Georgia Tech's demand; no Michigan law required it.

lessons.title: First Broadcasts and a Bracket
lessons.mainIdea: College games reached television in 1939, the same year a national basketball tournament began in Evanston, Illinois, and both grew into large businesses.
reading: On September 30, 1939, NBC's experimental station W2XBS televised a college football game between Fordham and Waynesburg in New York City. It is usually called the first televised football game. Very few homes had a television set, and the signal reached only the New York area.

The same year, the first national men's college basketball *tournament* was held. A tournament is a set of games that ends with one champion. Eight teams took part. The final was played at Patten Gymnasium on Northwestern's campus in Evanston, Illinois. Oregon beat Ohio State. The coaches' association ran it, and the NCAA soon took it over.

The field kept growing. It reached 64 teams in 1985 and 68 teams in 2011. CBS began broadcasting the final in 1982. In 2010, CBS and Turner signed a 14-year deal for the men's tournament worth about 10.8 billion dollars. *Broadcast rights* are the right to show a game on television or radio, which schools and leagues sell.

Money from the men's tournament became the NCAA's largest source of income. Much of it flows back to Division I conferences and schools. The NCAA women's tournament began in 1982 with 32 teams. Louisiana Tech won the first title. The women's field grew to 64 teams in 1994.

words.d: a set of games in which teams are eliminated until one champion is left
the right to show a game on radio, television or online, sold by schools and leagues
the full group of teams that enter a tournament

look.title: How Big the Men's Tournament Grew
look.cite: NCAA Division I men's basketball championship records
look.prompt: Between which two years shown did the field grow the most? Why might more teams mean more television money?

check.q: Where was the final of the first national men's college basketball tournament played in 1939?
choices: Madison Square Garden in New York
check.why: Oregon beat Ohio State at Northwestern's Patten Gymnasium in Evanston.

check.q: What are broadcast rights?
choices: the right to show a game on radio or television, which is sold
the right of fans to buy tickets
check.why: Schools, conferences and the NCAA sell the right to broadcast games.

check.q: How many teams were in the men's tournament field starting in 2011?
check.why: The field grew from 64 to 68 teams in 2011.

lessons.title: The Court and the TV Plan
lessons.mainIdea: In 1984 the Supreme Court ruled that the NCAA's limits on televised football broke federal antitrust law, and schools and conferences began selling their own games.
reading: Starting in 1951, the NCAA controlled how college football appeared on television. Its *television plan* limited how many games were shown and how often any one school could appear. The NCAA signed the contracts with the networks and shared the money among schools. Leaders feared that too much television would empty the stadiums.

Big football schools thought the plan held them back. In the late 1970s, many of them formed the College Football Association to push for their own deals. The University of Oklahoma and the University of Georgia sued the NCAA. They argued the plan was a form of price-fixing that federal law forbids.

*Antitrust law* protects competition in business. Its main federal law is the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890. On June 27, 1984, in NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 for the schools. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that the plan restrained competition in selling games to television.

After the ruling, conferences and schools sold their own games. Many more games reached television, and the price per game fell. The case also said the NCAA could keep some rules that protect amateur sport. Later lawsuits by players would lean on both parts of that decision.

words.d: law that protects competition in business and forbids agreements that fix prices or limit markets
the NCAA's system, begun in 1951, for limiting and selling televised college football games
an agreement among sellers to set a price instead of competing

look.title: The Court's Reasoning in 1984
look.text: The majority held that the NCAA's television plan limited the number of games shown and fixed the price networks paid. Those limits, it said, restrained competition and did not serve consumers. It added that some NCAA rules, such as those keeping players amateur, could still help make college sport possible.
look.cite: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, 468 U.S. 85 (1984), opinion of Justice Stevens
look.prompt: The Court struck down one NCAA rule but praised another kind. Why might later players' lawsuits quote both parts?

check.q: Which schools sued the NCAA over its football television plan?
check.why: The University of Oklahoma and the University of Georgia brought the case.

check.q: What does antitrust law protect?
choices: the right to form a conference
check.why: Antitrust law, such as the Sherman Act of 1890, protects competition.

check.q: What changed after the 1984 ruling?
choices: Schools and conferences sold their own games, and many more were shown.
check.why: Conferences and schools began selling their own broadcast rights.

lessons.title: Where "Student-Athlete" Came From
lessons.mainIdea: The NCAA adopted the term student-athlete in the 1950s, and its longtime leader later wrote that the term helped keep players from being treated as employees.
reading: Walter Byers led the NCAA as executive director from 1951 to 1987. He built its national office, its television contracts and its enforcement staff. Enforcement means investigating schools and punishing rule-breakers. Under Byers, the NCAA grew from a small rule-making group into a powerful national body.

In the 1950s, some injured college players asked for *workers' compensation*. That is money states require employers to pay workers hurt on the job. In 1953, the Colorado Supreme Court upheld such an award for Ernest Nemeth, a University of Denver football player injured in practice. Other courts ruled the other way in later cases.

The NCAA began using the word *student-athlete* in its rules and papers. In his 1995 book Unsportsmanlike Conduct: Exploiting College Athletes, Byers wrote that the NCAA crafted the term to answer the threat that players might be seen as employees. The word put student first and made no mention of work.

Words in rules can matter in court. When a judge must decide whether someone is an *employee*, the judge looks at pay, control and the kind of work done. Calling a player a student-athlete did not settle those questions. It did shape how the public talked about college sport for decades.

words.d: the NCAA's term for a college athlete, used since the 1950s
payments that state law requires employers to make to workers hurt on the job
a person who works for someone else under their control, usually for pay
investigating rule-breaking and handing out penalties

look.title: Byers Looks Back
look.text: Looking back on his career, Walter Byers wrote that the NCAA invented the term student-athlete in the 1950s. He said its purpose was to fight the idea that college players were employees who could claim workers' compensation.
look.cite: Walter Byers with Charles Hammer, Unsportsmanlike Conduct: Exploiting College Athletes, 1995
look.prompt: Why might it matter that this account comes from the NCAA's own former leader rather than from a critic?

check.q: Who led the NCAA from 1951 to 1987?
check.why: Walter Byers was the NCAA's executive director for 36 years.

check.q: What is workers' compensation?
choices: money employers must pay workers hurt on the job
a bonus for winning a title
check.why: Workers' compensation is required by state law for employees injured at work.

check.q: According to Byers, why did the NCAA craft the term student-athlete?
choices: to answer the threat that players might be seen as employees
to replace the word amateur in the Olympics
check.why: Byers wrote in 1995 that the term was meant to counter employee claims.

lessons.title: Players Take the NCAA to Court
lessons.mainIdea: In O'Bannon (2014–2015) and Alston (2021), courts ruled that some NCAA limits on what players receive broke antitrust law.
reading: Ed O'Bannon won a national title with UCLA in 1995. Years later he saw a player who looked like him in a college basketball video game. He had never agreed to it or been paid. In 2009 he sued the NCAA over the use of players' *names, images and likenesses*. A likeness is a picture or copy that clearly shows a person.

In August 2014, federal judge Claudia Wilken ruled that NCAA rules barring such payments broke antitrust law. In 2015 a federal appeals court agreed in part. It allowed schools to cover the full cost of attendance. It struck down her plan to let schools hold up to 5,000 dollars a year for each player.

Shawne Alston, a former West Virginia football player, led the next major case. On June 21, 2021, in NCAA v. Alston, the Supreme Court ruled 9 to 0 against the NCAA. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that the NCAA could not cap *education-related benefits*, such as computers, study abroad or paid internships.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a separate opinion that went further. He said other NCAA pay limits might also break antitrust law. He wrote that the NCAA is not above the law. His opinion was not the ruling of the Court, but lawyers and lawmakers quoted it widely.

words.d: a person's name, picture and identity, which can be used to sell things; often shortened to NIL
things tied to schooling, such as computers, study abroad or graduate scholarships
a separate opinion by a judge who agrees with the ruling but adds reasons of their own

look.title: One Ruling, Two Opinions
look.text: June 2021. Nine justices agree that the NCAA may not cap education-related benefits. The main opinion stops there. One justice writes separately. He says the NCAA's other pay limits may also be illegal, and that its business model would be illegal in almost any other industry.
look.prompt: Which opinion is binding law, and which is a signal? Why might a separate opinion still change what happens next?

check.q: What did Ed O'Bannon sue over?
choices: the use of players' names, images and likenesses without pay
check.why: O'Bannon objected to a video game using his likeness without consent or pay.

check.q: How did the Supreme Court rule in NCAA v. Alston (2021)?
choices: It refused to hear the case.
check.why: The Court was unanimous that the NCAA could not cap education-related benefits.

check.q: What is a concurring opinion?
choices: a rule written by the NCAA
a judge's separate opinion that agrees with the ruling and adds reasons
check.why: Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence agreed with the ruling and went further.

lessons.title: A Union Vote in Evanston
lessons.mainIdea: Northwestern football players sought a union in 2014; a regional labor official agreed they were employees, but the national labor board declined to decide in 2015.
reading: A *union* is a group of workers who join together to bargain with an employer over pay and conditions. In January 2014, Northwestern University football players asked the National Labor Relations Board to recognize a union. The *NLRB* is the federal agency that oversees union elections for private employers. Quarterback Kain Colter was a leader of the effort.

The players worked with the College Athletes Players Association. It was linked to the National College Players Association, an advocacy group founded by Ramogi Huma, a former UCLA player. The players said they worked long hours under coaches' control in exchange for scholarships. Northwestern said they were students first.

On March 26, 2014, NLRB regional director Peter Ohr ruled that Northwestern's scholarship football players were employees. The players voted in April 2014, but the ballots were sealed while the university appealed. On August 17, 2015, the national board declined to take the case. It said a ruling for one private school could upset balance in a league of mostly public schools.

The question did not go away. In September 2021, the NLRB's general counsel wrote that some college athletes can be employees. In 2024, Dartmouth men's basketball players voted 13 to 2 to join a union after a regional director ruled them employees. Northwestern is a private school, so federal labor law reached it; public universities fall under state labor laws instead.

words.d: a group of workers who join together to bargain with an employer
the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that oversees union elections at private employers
talks between a union and an employer to agree on pay and working conditions

look.title: Sealed Ballots
look.text: Evanston, April 2014. Scholarship football players vote on whether to form a union. The votes are cast, then locked away uncounted while the university appeals. More than a year later, the national board says it will not decide the case. The ballots are never counted.
look.prompt: Who decided the question in the end: the players, the university or the board? What did the board's choice leave open?

check.q: What is the NLRB?
choices: the federal agency that oversees union elections at private employers
check.why: The National Labor Relations Board handles union elections for private employers.

check.q: What did the regional director rule in March 2014?
choices: Northwestern players were amateurs, not employees.
Northwestern's scholarship football players were employees.

check.why: Peter Ohr ruled on March 26, 2014, that the scholarship players were employees.

check.q: Why did federal labor law reach Northwestern but not most public universities?
choices: Northwestern is in the Big Ten.
Northwestern is a private school; public schools fall under state labor laws.
check.why: The NLRB covers private employers; public universities fall under state law.

lessons.title: Getting Paid for a Name
lessons.mainIdea: State laws in 2019–2021 let college athletes earn money from their names, and a 2025 court settlement let schools pay athletes directly.
reading: On September 30, 2019, California governor Gavin Newsom signed the Fair Pay to Play Act. It said college athletes in California could earn money from their *NIL*, meaning name, image and likeness. Other states passed similar laws. Illinois passed its own law, the Student-Athlete Endorsement Rights Act, in 2021.

Several state laws took effect on July 1, 2021. That same day, the NCAA adopted an interim policy letting athletes in every state earn NIL money. An *endorsement* is a deal in which a person is paid to promote a product. Athletes signed deals with local businesses, apparel brands and social-media sponsors.

Groups of boosters soon formed *collectives*. A collective pools money from fans and donors to pay athletes at one school for NIL work. Critics said collectives worked like hidden salaries. Supporters said athletes were finally sharing in money their fame had always helped raise.

A class-action lawsuit named for Arizona State swimmer Grant House went further. On June 6, 2025, Judge Claudia Wilken approved a settlement. It set about 2.8 billion dollars in back damages for former athletes. It also let Division I schools share revenue directly with athletes, up to about 20.5 million dollars per school in the first year.

words.d: name, image and likeness; a person's identity used to promote or sell something
a deal in which a person is paid to promote a product or business
a group that pools money from fans and donors to pay athletes at one school for NIL work
an agreement that ends a lawsuit without a full trial

look.title: Steps Toward Paying College Athletes
rows: California Fair Pay to Play Act signed

look.prompt: How many years passed from the first lawsuit to direct payments by schools? Which step came from a legislature rather than a court?

check.q: What does NIL stand for?
check.why: NIL means a person's name, image and likeness.

check.q: What happened on July 1, 2021?
choices: State NIL laws took effect and the NCAA let athletes everywhere earn NIL money.
Northwestern players voted on a union.
check.why: Several state laws took effect that day, and the NCAA adopted an interim NIL policy.

check.q: What did the 2025 House settlement allow?
choices: Players to form a national union
Division I schools to share revenue directly with athletes
the NCAA to end all scholarships
check.why: The settlement let schools pay athletes directly, up to about 20.5 million dollars in the first year.

review.q: Which body did colleges create in 1906 in response to football deaths?
choices: the IAAUS, renamed the NCAA in 1910
review.why: The IAAUS formed on March 31, 1906, and became the NCAA in 1910.

review.q: What made the Western Conference of 1895 different from student-run sport?
choices: Professors from each school made the rules.
It was run by a railroad.
It allowed only freshmen to play.
review.why: The conference was built on faculty control.

review.q: What did the 1929 Carnegie report find?
choices: College sport had no money problems.
Many colleges recruited and secretly paid athletes.
review.why: Howard Savage's team found widespread recruiting and hidden payments.

review.q: Which case ended the NCAA's control of televised college football?
choices: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma
review.why: The 1984 ruling said the television plan broke antitrust law.

review.q: Why does the Nemeth case of 1953 matter to the student-or-worker question?
choices: A court upheld workers' compensation for an injured college player.
review.why: Colorado's Supreme Court treated an injured player's claim like a worker's claim.

review.q: How did the NLRB end the Northwestern union case in 2015?
choices: It declined to take the case.
It sent the case to the NCAA.
review.why: The board declined jurisdiction on August 17, 2015, and the ballots were never counted.

review.q: Which pair is in the correct order, earliest first?
choices: Title IX, then the AIAW is founded
Proposition 48, then the first athletic scholarships
Harvard–Yale rowing race, then Rutgers–Princeton football game
NIL laws, then the O'Bannon lawsuit
review.why: The rowing race was in 1852 and the football game in 1869.

review.q: What is the difference between a scholarship and revenue sharing under the 2025 settlement?
choices: A scholarship is paid by fans; revenue sharing by the NCAA.
A scholarship is illegal; revenue sharing is required.
A scholarship pays for school; revenue sharing is money paid directly to the athlete.
review.why: Scholarships cover the cost of school, while the settlement let schools also pay athletes directly.
